The experimental apparatus was designed and developed at the MIT Gas Turbine Laboratory.
The blade model simulates the leading edge geometry of a real turbine blade and rotates in a vacuum chamber.
The local heat transfer coefficients are determined from the measured electrical input power and the skin temperature distribution.
The flows in the supply and impingement regions are both modeled as steady state channel flows, using friction and heat transfer coefficients.
The maximum difference between the Nusselt numbers calculated using the local fluid temperature versus the inlet coolant temperature is 17 percent.
Rotation reduces the mean Nusselt numbers by about 30 percent compared to the non-rotating impingement results of Chupp.
The heat transfer rate is lower at 0 degrees stagger angle by approximately 30% compared to the 30 degree stagger angle.
As the average jet Reynolds number varies from 17,000 to 74,000, the heat transfer rate increases by about a factor of 3.
The temperature ratio between the average skin temperature and the coolant temperature has almost no effect on the Nusselt number.
The modeling reveals important radial variations in the Nusselt number distributions due to rotation.
The effects of stagger angle on the thermal gradients between the impingement jets are significant.
The channel flow modeling approach is validated by comparing the calculated Nusselt numbers to correlations from other investigators.
The modeling and analysis offer a means for more accurate prediction of impingement cooling heat transfer rates.
The experimental apparatus includes a vacuum chamber to reduce heat transfer by convection and eliminate any absorbing medium.
